title: Only one arrow
hookLine: the untaught feel pain and then a second arrow of distress (SN 36.6)

lines: A STUBBED TOE AT SIX A.M.
cards: You stub your toe on the bed frame at six in the morning. That's the pain. Then, within half a second: who put this bed here, why does this always happen to me, this whole day is ruined.

And then, if you're like a lot of people, you reach for something to make it go away: your phone, a snack, an hour of a show. Three moves, one tiny injury. The second arrow may be familiar from year one.
But the discourse it comes from keeps going past the second arrow, to that third move.

teach.h: THE SAME FEELINGS, A DIFFERENT RESPONSE
teach.b: SN 36.6 is called the Arrow. The Buddha asks the monks: the untaught person feels pleasant, painful and neutral feelings. So does the well-taught disciple.
What's the difference? Then the picture. Touched by a painful feeling, the untaught person sorrows, grieves, laments, beats their chest, and becomes distraught.
So they feel two feelings, one in the body and one in the mind.

teach.h: A SECOND ARROW IN THE SAME PLACE
teach.b: It's as if a man were struck by an arrow, and then a second arrow hit him in the same place. Here's the part that's often skipped. Touched by pain, the text says, the untaught person seeks delight in sensual pleasure.
Why? Because they know no other way out of painful feeling.

teach.h: NO OTHER WAY OUT BUT PLEASURE
teach.b: So pain leads to resistance, resistance leads to reaching for pleasure, and the pleasure feeds a habit of wanting.
The discourse names three underlying tendencies stirred up along the way: toward aversion, toward lust, and toward not seeing clearly. A whole cycle, from one stubbed toe.
The well-taught disciple, touched by the same pain, doesn't sorrow, lament or become distraught. They feel one feeling, the bodily one. One arrow.
And because they know another way out of pain than pleasure, they don't need to reach. Notice what the text doesn't promise.
The first arrow still lands, even on the well-taught.
The body still hurts. What changes is everything that usually comes after.

how: Some Buddhist teachers use the arrow simile in teaching about pain and illness, and some modern mindfulness programs for chronic pain draw on the distinction between physical pain and the distress added to it.

o: a bow drawn back to shoot
a wound that will never heal
an arrow or dart that strikes

s: the well-taught disciple stops feeling bodily pain
the first arrow still lands; what drops away is the second.
SN 36.6 says the untaught reach for pleasure to escape pain
because they know no other way out of painful feeling.
the discourse names three underlying tendencies
toward aversion, toward lust, and toward not seeing clearly.

games.q: a painful feeling has just hit you. according to SN 36.6, what does the untaught person do next?
o: grieve and lament, then reach for sensual pleasure.
feel it plainly and let it pass.
games.why: the untaught add a second arrow of distress, then look for pleasure, because they know no other escape.

practice: Find one small discomfort in the body right now, a tight back, a restless leg, and feel it plainly: where it is, its size, whether it pulses or stays; that's the first arrow.
Watch for the second, a thought like I hate this, and for the third, the urge to fix it with something nice. If either comes, notice it, and come back to just the sensation.

wordCard.voice: Salla. The Pali word for an arrow or dart, the image in SN 36.6: the well-taught feel the body's pain without the second arrow of distress, and without reaching for pleasure as the only way out. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali salla: an arrow or dart. SN 36.6 is the Sallatha Sutta, the arrow.

carryVoice: Your line: one arrow lands, not two. The body may still hurt; the rest is what can change. See you tomorrow.
